claims.text: The starting material is a noble-metal-based high-entropy alloy with an equimolar composition.
The precursor has homogeneous elemental mixing.
Rapid quenching kinetically traps a high-entropy metastable nanoalloy structure.
Rapid quenching produces a higher density of catalytically active defects.
Slow cooling promotes defect annealing and consequently lowers defect density.
A retained single-phase structure and high defect density provide more catalytically active sites.
Rapidly quenched HEA nanomaterials will have statistically significantly greater catalytic activity than slow-cooled controls.
Rapidly quenched HEA nanomaterials will have statistically significantly greater catalytic selectivity than slow-cooled controls.
The predicted catalytic improvement is caused by higher defect density and retention of a single-phase structure.
The slow-cooled baseline will exhibit partial phase segregation and lower defect density.
The hypothesis is intended to apply only within a narrowly defined compositional window and controlled catalytic synthesis conditions.
The quantitative relationship between defect density and catalytic performance may depend on alloy composition and reaction conditions.

The hypothesis is falsified if rapid quenching fails to increase both defect density and catalytic performance significantly relative to the slow-cooled control, or if slow cooling gives superior performance.
